_note: The people of Mirefen and their conversations (prop dialogues included).

npcs.name: Reeve Tamsin Lowe
npcs.title: Reeve of Lowlantern
npcs.bark: Mind the third plank. And the seventh. Actually, mind all the planks.

npcs.name: Obadiah Wick
npcs.title: Lanternwright
npcs.bark: Glass, wick, glow. Glass, wick, glow. That's all a lantern is. That's all anything is, really.

npcs.name: Hettie Brine
npcs.title: Fen Goods and Chowder
npcs.bark: Chowder! Fresh chowder! Only slightly crocolisk!

npcs.name: Lily
npcs.title: Duchess of the Puddles
npcs.bark: Have you seen a frog? Very handsome. Answers to 'Your Grace'.

npcs.name: Bo Puddlefoot
npcs.title: Fisherman
npcs.bark: Nine fingers, three boats, no nets. Ask me how. Actually, don't.

npcs.name: Old Corwin
npcs.title: Once of the Heronguard
npcs.bark: The fen's quiet. I like it quiet. Quiet doesn't ask you where the other twenty-nine are.

npcs.name: Granny Sen
npcs.title: A Lantern That Didn't Go Out
npcs.bark: Hm. You've got wet feet and a good face. That'll do.

npcs.name: Old Bloop-Who-Listens
npcs.title: Mireling Oracle (Exiled)
npcs.bark: Bloop listens. Bloop always listens. Nobody listens to Bloop.

npcs.name: Ansel Reedcutter
npcs.title: Reedcutter
npcs.bark: Reeds for thatch, reeds for baskets, reeds for the lanterns' wicks. Reeds for everything, except boats. Learned that one the hard way.

npcs.name: Orla Netmender
npcs.title: Netmender
npcs.bark: Over, under, knot. Over, under, knot. Bo, if that crocolisk eats one more of these I'm mending you.

npcs.name: Plip
npcs.title: Mireling Trader (Very Official)
npcs.bark: Plip sells! Plip buys! Plip is Gubbagulp's nephew, so Plip has the best prices. Plip decided this.

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *A tall woman in a reed hat is nailing a ledger to a post with the air of someone who has nailed many ledgers to many posts. She looks you over, boots first.* Dry feet. Clean cloak. You're not from the fen, and you're not lost, which makes you rare.

nodes.speaker: mf_reeve_tamsin
nodes.text: Tamsin Lowe, Reeve of Lowlantern. That means I count the planks, settle the arguments and get blamed for the weather. Mind the third plank. And the seventh. Actually, mind all of them.

nodes.speaker: mf_reeve_tamsin
nodes.text: Well? What can Lowlantern do for you — or, more likely, what can you do for Lowlantern?

choices.text: Archivist Penhallow of Brightwater sent me. Something is drowning your lanterns.
I cut these from the drowned lanterns. They were knotted round their feet.
Tell me about the drowned lanterns again.
Where do I find Auntie Gall?
Auntie Gall is gone. The coven's ring is broken.
You look like a woman with a frog problem.
I've already been to the Croaking Stones. Gubbagulp and I have... come to an understanding.
Gubbagulp won't be cutting your lines again.
Is anyone paying for coven hags?
The coven is five hags fewer. About that bounty.

nodes.speaker: mf_reeve_tamsin
nodes.text: *She stops hammering.* Penhallow. That old owl still remembers us? Good. Then you'll want the whole of it. When someone in the fen dies, we float a lantern out on the Sinking Mere, and the tide-singer sings it away to the deep marsh. That's a sending. For a year now, every lantern has sunk before the song is done.

nodes.speaker: mf_reeve_tamsin
nodes.text: Our tide-singer is a girl called Nanami. She thinks it's her fault, because it started with her grandmother's sending — Granny Sen's. It isn't her fault. I'd bet the village on it. But I can't prove it, and I can't walk out to the Mere every night and stare at the water.

choices.text: Then I'll go and stare at it for you.
You said 'sinks'. Not 'goes out'. Lanterns don't sink on their own.

nodes.speaker: mf_reeve_tamsin
nodes.text: *Her mouth goes thin.* No. They don't. Somebody's pulling them. I've thought it a hundred nights and said it to nobody, because the only somebodies out in that water are frogs, crocolisks and Mother Mire's daughters. And I don't fancy any of those answers.

nodes.speaker: mf_reeve_tamsin
nodes.text: *She shrugs.* Water's water. Things go into it. That's most of what water's for.

nodes.speaker: mf_reeve_tamsin
nodes.text: The Sinking Mere is west along the Fen Road — follow the lamp-posts, the ones that still work. There's a boardwalk straight across it. Look at the lanterns properly. Whatever you find, bring it back to me.

nodes.speaker: mf_reeve_tamsin
nodes.text: West along the Fen Road to the Sinking Mere, and out along the boardwalk. Three of the old sending-lanterns stand right beside the planks. Look at their feet. Look at everything. Then come back.

nodes.speaker: mf_reeve_tamsin
nodes.text: *She takes the cords and turns one over. The frog-bone charms click together. Every bit of colour leaves her face.* Coven knots. Mother Mire's daughters tie these. A drowning cord: tie it to a stone, loop it on the lantern's foot, and anything you float there gets pulled down.

nodes.speaker: mf_reeve_tamsin
nodes.text: Somebody has been sinking our dead on purpose. For a year. *She sits down on an upturned crate, quite suddenly.* The coven gathers at the old moon-gate in the north-west, past the Croaking Stones. Their eldest is Auntie Gall. If anybody holds the other end of these cords, it's her.

choices.text: Why would a coven want drowned lanterns?
Then I'll go and have a word with Auntie Gall.

nodes.speaker: mf_reeve_tamsin
nodes.text: Why does a coven want anything? Old stories say the moon-gate opens on the deep places, where the Hollow Heart beats. Lights go down, something down there gets fed. *She spits in the water, very precisely.* That's a story for children. I hope.

nodes.speaker: mf_reeve_tamsin
nodes.text: Go at dusk, if you can stand it — that's when the ring is busiest. Take friends. Take more friends than you think. And whatever Auntie Gall offers you, don't drink it.

nodes.speaker: mf_reeve_tamsin
nodes.text: North-west, past the Croaking Stones, along the old road to the moon-gate. Look for green fire and a lot of hats. She'll be the one in the middle who is enjoying herself.

nodes.speaker: mf_reeve_tamsin
nodes.text: *She closes her eyes for a long moment.* Then the Mere can let go. Go out there tonight. I think — *she laughs, a little shakily* — I think someone on the boardwalk has been waiting for you. Nanami doesn't know. Don't you dare tell her before it's done.

nodes.speaker: mf_reeve_tamsin
nodes.text: You'll see. The fen keeps what it loves, a little longer than it should. *She waves you off.* Go on. The Mere, the boardwalk, the middle.

nodes.speaker: mf_reeve_tamsin
nodes.text: *She is standing on the porch with her hat off, watching the west, where a hundred little lights are drifting on the Mere like a tide of stars.* I counted them. I always count them. Every one is floating. *She wipes her face with the back of her hand.* Lowlantern won't forget this. I'll see to it.

nodes.speaker: mf_reeve_tamsin
nodes.text: I've a mireling problem, which is a frog problem with ambitions. Somebody's been cutting our fishing lines and stealing the glass out of our lamps. It's Gubbagulp's lot, from the Croaking Stones. Their chief. Big. Shiny crown. Opinions.

choices.text: I'll go and talk to him.

nodes.speaker: mf_reeve_tamsin
nodes.text: Then do the other thing. I'm not squeamish. But mirelings were our neighbours long before the coven started whispering at them, and I'd rather have neighbours than a hole where they used to be.

choices.text: I'll see what I can do.

nodes.speaker: mf_reeve_tamsin
nodes.text: South-west, past the Heron Bridge. Follow the croaking. You can't miss it; nobody ever has.

nodes.speaker: mf_reeve_tamsin
nodes.text: *Her eyebrows climb right up under her hat.* Already? Gubbagulp? Well, I'll write that in the ledger. In ink.

nodes.speaker: mf_reeve_tamsin
nodes.text: So? How did it go?

nodes.speaker: mf_reeve_tamsin
nodes.text: *You tell her. She listens with her head on one side, and when you hand her Gubbagulp's pearl she holds it up to the light for a long time.* A pearl. From Gubbagulp. Forty years I've lived on this pool and the mirelings have never given us so much as a wet look. If they want to trade, we'll trade. If they want to come to the lantern-night, they can come.

nodes.speaker: mf_reeve_tamsin
nodes.text: *She looks at the pearl from the chief's crown, and then at you, and nods slowly.* So it came to that. Well. The lines will stay whole. I'll put the pearl in the Reeve's box, and tell the children there was a big frog and he lost.

nodes.speaker: mf_reeve_tamsin
nodes.text: Here. The village's thanks, such as they are — and they are, I promise, considerable.

nodes.speaker: mf_reeve_tamsin
nodes.text: Paying? I'll pay in coin, in chowder and in the undying gratitude of every fisher on this pool. The coven's daughters are still out there in their hats, tying cords. Five of them fewer would let a lot of people sleep.

nodes.speaker: mf_reeve_tamsin
nodes.text: They prowl the road to the moon-gate, the reeds by the sunken statue, and anywhere a lantern used to be. Mind the frogs on their hats. The frogs are the clever ones.

nodes.speaker: mf_reeve_tamsin
nodes.text: *She counts out the coins twice, then a third time out of habit.* Five fewer hats. The fishers will sing your name. Badly, but loudly.

nodes.speaker: mf_reeve_tamsin
nodes.text: Lowlantern's been on this pool since before Brightwater had a bridge. Stilts, because the fen moves. Boardwalks, because the fen bites. And lanterns — every porch has a hook. One for the living, so the boats find home. One for the dead, on the Mere. Lately most of the hooks are empty.

choices.text: Who lives out in the fen besides you?
Let me ask about something else.

nodes.speaker: mf_reeve_tamsin
nodes.text: Because nobody wants to light a lantern and watch it sink. Grief's heavy enough without the water pulling at it. Mother Wren at the Chapel of Small Lights in Brightwater still sends us a box of candles every winter. We've stopped opening them.

nodes.speaker: mf_reeve_tamsin
nodes.text: Mirelings at the Croaking Stones — frog-folk, mostly harmless, lately less so. Crocolisks in the Shallows. Something unpleasant in the Drowned Barrows. An old knight called Corwin who lives out there and talks to nobody. And Mother Mire's coven, who we don't talk about, except all the time.

nodes.speaker: mf_reeve_tamsin
nodes.text: Our tide-singer, before Nanami. Sharp as a heron and twice as bossy. She taught half this village to swim and the other half to mind its manners. She died last winter. Her lantern was the first to sink. *She looks away across the pool.* Nanami was singing it. She hasn't forgiven herself.

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *A round man in a leather apron is squinting at a lantern through three pairs of spectacles worn at once. The workshop behind him clinks with glass. Everything smells of lamp oil and toast.*

nodes.speaker: mf_obi_wick
nodes.text: Obadiah Wick, lanternwright. Obi, if you're in a hurry, and everybody is. Glass, wick, glow — that's all a lantern is. Mind you, that's all anything is, if you squint.

nodes.speaker: mf_obi_wick
nodes.text: *Obi takes off one pair of spectacles, then the other two.* What can I light for you?

choices.text: Five lumps of fen-glass and four wisp-glows, as ordered.
Where do I find fen-glass and wisp-glow again?
What will you make with all that glass?
I'm one lamp short. Do you have another?
The Fen Road is lit, all the way to the Croaking Stones.
Why do the lanterns matter so much to you?
Wisp-glow isn't fire, is it? It's something else.

nodes.speaker: mf_obi_wick
nodes.text: Short? We're starving! Half the village won't light a lamp, and the other half can't — the mirelings have been pinching the glass out of them. They collect it, you see. Like magpies, but wetter. Bring me fen-glass, and a little wisp-glow for the wicks, and I'll make lanterns that stay lit.

nodes.speaker: mf_obi_wick
nodes.text: Five good lumps of glass — the mirelings of the Croaking Stones carry it in their pouches — and four drops of wisp-glow. The fen wisps leave it behind when they... stop. Round the Mere, and in Willow Hollow.

nodes.speaker: mf_obi_wick
nodes.text: Splendid! Bring it back in one piece. Or several pieces. Glass is glass; I melt it anyway.

nodes.speaker: mf_obi_wick
nodes.text: Glass from the mirelings, down at the Croaking Stones, south-west past the Heron Bridge. Glow from the wisps — round the Sinking Mere, and up in Willow Hollow among the big toadstools. Wisps are pretty. Wisps also bite. Keep that in mind.

nodes.speaker: mf_obi_wick
nodes.text: *He tips the glass onto the bench and holds a wisp-glow up to his spectacles. It wriggles.* Oh, that's lovely. That's very, very lovely. Give me a night and a full kettle and you'll see something.

nodes.speaker: mf_obi_wick
nodes.text: *He sets four lamps on the bench: green glass, fat wicks, a drop of glow trembling in each.* Post-lamps! The Fen Road's been dark since the coven's lot started smashing them. Hang these on the four dead posts between here and the Croaking Stones, and the fen folk can walk to the Mere at night again.

nodes.speaker: mf_obi_wick
nodes.text: The first dead post is by the turning to the Shallows. Then the Mere road, then the Heron Bridge, then the last one by the Croaking Stones. That last one's in coven country. Something always notices when a light comes on.

nodes.speaker: mf_obi_wick
nodes.text: *He looks at you over all three pairs of spectacles.* You dropped one in the fen, didn't you. Everybody does. Here.

nodes.speaker: mf_obi_wick
nodes.text: I saw them! From the porch! Four little green stars, all down the road. *He has to take his spectacles off to wipe them.* Old Tobben in Lanternvale used to say a lantern isn't for seeing by. It's for being seen. I never knew what he meant till tonight.

nodes.speaker: mf_obi_wick
nodes.text: Because out here the dark goes on for miles, and a lantern on a porch says: somebody lives here, somebody's waiting, come home. And on the Mere it says: we haven't forgotten you. That's a lot of work for a bit of glass and a wick. I like to make sure it's good glass.

nodes.speaker: mf_obi_wick
nodes.text: *His eyebrows shoot up.* Exactly! It's the memory of light. A wisp is what's left when a lantern goes out somewhere it shouldn't have. That's why their glow takes so kindly to a new wick. It wants to be a lantern again.

nodes.speaker: mf_obi_wick
nodes.text: *You say something learned about phosphorescence. Obi nods politely, the way people nod at a cat bringing them a leaf.*

nodes.speaker: mf_hettie_brine
nodes.text: *A broad woman behind a stall of jars, nets and a bubbling pot waves a ladle at you.* Customer! A real one, with coin and everything. Hettie Brine. Fen goods, potions that mostly work, and the best chowder in Mirefen. It's also the only chowder in Mirefen. Don't tell anyone.

nodes.speaker: mf_hettie_brine
nodes.text: What'll it be, love?

choices.text: Four crocolisk tails and three fen truffles, chef.
Who's the old knight out by the barrows?

nodes.speaker: mf_hettie_brine
nodes.text: Ambitious is right. It's lantern-night chowder — or it will be, once there's a lantern-night again. Proper Mire Chowder wants crocolisk tail, four of them, and fen truffles, three. Bring me those and I'll feed the whole pool.

nodes.speaker: mf_hettie_brine
nodes.text: Really! It's like chicken, if the chicken had tried to eat you first. That's what gives it the flavour. Spite.

nodes.speaker: mf_hettie_brine
nodes.text: Crocs in the Gnashing Shallows and anywhere there's a sunny log. Truffles grow under the giant toadstools in Willow Hollow — dig at the roots, gently. If it smells like rain on a cellar door, it's a truffle. If it smells like feet, it's a foot.

nodes.speaker: mf_hettie_brine
nodes.text: Truffles under the big toadstools in Willow Hollow, north-east of the pool. Croc tails from crocs. That bit's simple. The crocs will disagree.

nodes.speaker: mf_hettie_brine
nodes.text: *She sniffs a truffle and closes her eyes in something close to prayer.* Oh, you beauty. *Into the pot it all goes. The steam turns gold.* Here — take a few bowls for the road, and this, and don't argue. Nobody argues with a woman holding a ladle.

nodes.speaker: mf_hettie_brine
nodes.text: Corwin. Came down out of the north twelve years ago with a heron on his coat and a look in his eye like a door that won't shut. Lives out past the Mere with the ghosts. Buys fish-hooks and nothing else. Never says a word about Skyreach, which is how you know it's the only thing he thinks about.

nodes.speaker: mf_hettie_brine
nodes.text: *She leans in.* Love, a good cook never tells. A great cook tells you, and then you never eat it again. I am a very good cook.

nodes.speaker: mf_lily
nodes.text: *Lily is wearing a lily-pad hat. Under it, something croaks.* The Duke sends his regards. He's in here. He likes it in here. It's warm.

nodes.speaker: mf_lily
nodes.text: I visit the Duke on Sundays. Lady Bubbles makes him very happy. *She sighs a great sigh.* It is so romantic I could be sick.

nodes.speaker: mf_lily
nodes.text: *Lily grabs your sleeve with both hands.* Did you find him? Is he alright? Is he SOUP?

choices.text: Not soup. Here he is — His Grace, safe and sound.
He's safe. But he's not coming home, Lily. Let me explain.

nodes.speaker: mf_lily
nodes.text: *You open your hands. The Duke of Puddles regards Lily with enormous dignity, then leaps onto her head.* YOUR GRACE! *She is crying and laughing and he is croaking and it is, frankly, a lot.* Thank you thank you thank you. You can have anything. Not him. Anything else.

nodes.speaker: mf_lily
nodes.text: *You explain about the stewpot, and the rescue, and Lady Bubbles, and how the Duke looked at her. Lily listens very seriously.* ...So he's in love. *A long pause.* A duke has to follow his heart. That's in all the books. *She sniffles, very bravely.* Can I visit?

nodes.speaker: mf_lily
nodes.text: Any clues? He likes mushroom rings, and willows, and anywhere with flies. He is very handsome. He has a little crown. Well, a spot that looks like a crown.

nodes.speaker: mf_lily
nodes.text: *A girl in an enormous raincoat is peering under the boardwalk.* Your Grace? Your GRACE? *She notices you.* Oh! Are you a knight? You've got the shoulders of a knight.

nodes.speaker: mf_lily
nodes.text: That's what knights say when they're being modest. I've read about it.

nodes.speaker: mf_lily
nodes.text: His Grace the Duke of Puddles! My frog. He's been gone two days, which is a hundred years in frog. I'm not allowed past the Fen Road on my own because of the crocolisks and the hags and the ghosts and the everything. Will you look for him?

nodes.speaker: mf_lily
nodes.text: Green. Shiny. Very handsome. He answers to 'Your Grace', but only if he's in the mood.

nodes.speaker: mf_lily
nodes.text: THANK you. He loves the fairy ring up in Willow Hollow. Start there. If he's not there, he's somewhere else. That's how frogs work.

nodes.speaker: mf_bo_puddlefoot
nodes.text: *Bo is mending a net with Orla's spare needle and humming.* Shallows are quiet. First fish in a month this morning. Ate it standing up. Best fish of my life.

nodes.speaker: mf_bo_puddlefoot
nodes.text: You're back! And you've still got all your fingers. Count them for me. Go on.

choices.text: Old Gnasher's done. The Shallows are yours again.

nodes.speaker: mf_bo_puddlefoot
nodes.text: *He sits down on his own dock, hard.* Gnasher. Done. Twenty years that log's been watching me. *He laughs, then can't stop laughing.* Here. Take your pick. I'd give you a boat, but you'd only get eaten in it.

nodes.speaker: mf_bo_puddlefoot
nodes.text: The crocs are in the Gnashing Shallows, south of the road. The big one, Gnasher, lies on the mud bank at the west end and pretends to be a log. He's not a log. I checked. That's how I lost the finger.

nodes.speaker: mf_bo_puddlefoot
nodes.text: *A wiry man in a reed hat is staring at a net that has been reduced to an idea of a net.* Nine fingers, three boats, no nets. Ask me how. Actually, don't.

choices.text: You should learn to read croc sign.

nodes.speaker: mf_bo_puddlefoot
nodes.text: *He squints at you.* You've the look of somebody who has. Go on, then. *You show him the slide-marks in the mud, the bubble-trails, the way the reeds lean.* ...Huh. They've been coming up the channel at dawn. All this time I've been fishing at dawn.

nodes.speaker: mf_bo_puddlefoot
nodes.text: Crocolisks. The Shallows are thick with them, and the biggest — Old Gnasher — has every net I own wrapped round his teeth like a scarf. Thin them out and see off Gnasher, and you can have the pick of my spare gear. I've a lot of spare gear. I've had a lot of bad days.

nodes.speaker: mf_bo_puddlefoot
nodes.text: Five of the small ones, then Gnasher. Mind the logs. Especially the logs that blink.

nodes.speaker: mf_bo_puddlefoot
nodes.text: Oldest croc in the fen. My grandad tried to catch him with a rope and a goose. He kept the rope. The goose kept Grandad's hat. Gnasher kept the goose.

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *An old man in a faded river-blue surcoat sits by a small fire, mending a boot. There is a heron on his breast, worked in white thread gone grey. He doesn't look up.* You're not from the fen. Nobody from the fen walks that straight.

nodes.speaker: mf_corwin
nodes.text: *Corwin pokes the fire.* Well. Say what you came to say. The fire doesn't mind company. I'm still deciding.

choices.text: That's a Heronguard heron on your coat.
What keeps you out here, with the ghosts?
Where do I find the bog ghouls?
Tell me about the Low Bell.
The barrows are quiet. The Bellringer sleeps.
Ysolde of the Heronguard says hello.

nodes.speaker: mf_corwin
nodes.text: *He looks down at it as if he'd forgotten.* It was. The Heronguard: forty knights under Lord-Commander Aubric, sworn to bring folk home from wherever they'd wandered. Twelve years ago we rode to Skyreach. Eleven of us came back. *He goes back to the boot.* I came back the furthest. All the way to the bottom of a swamp.

choices.text: Let me ask about something else.

nodes.speaker: mf_corwin
nodes.text: Fire. Fire that walked about in armour and called itself sworn. And under the mountain, something that breathed it out in its sleep. We never saw it. We only felt the stone get warm under our boots. *Long pause.* Aubric went forward to see. He didn't come back to tell us.

choices.text: Something under the mountain. A dragon?
Let me ask about something else.

nodes.speaker: mf_corwin
nodes.text: Don't say that word round here. The fen's superstitious. *But he nods, once.* If you ever go north, you'll find twenty-nine heron banners under the snow. Straighten one for me.

nodes.speaker: mf_corwin
nodes.text: *A grunt.* Don't be. Be careful. It's more use.

nodes.speaker: mf_corwin
nodes.text: *He stands up so fast the boot goes in the fire.* Ysolde? Little Ysolde, with the heron? Sir Wadsworth? *He fishes the boot out, swearing gently.* She was a squire when we rode north. Left her at the gate because she was too young. She cried for a week. *He looks at her, and at you.* Look at her now.

nodes.speaker: mf_corwin
nodes.text: Somebody has to keep the barrows. The fen folk bury their dead out there, on the mounds, and lately the fen's been giving them back. Bog ghouls — just mud and grief and somebody's old coat. They didn't ask to get up. Somebody has to put them down kindly.

choices.text: I'll help you lay them down.

nodes.speaker: mf_corwin
nodes.text: Same reason the lanterns sink, I'd wager. Something's pulling at the fen from underneath. The dead feel it first. They always do.

choices.text: I'll help you lay them down.

nodes.speaker: mf_corwin
nodes.text: Six of them, to start. They wander the mounds and the north shore of the Mere. Then ring the Low Bell — the old bronze in the broken arch. It used to call the dead home. Whatever's left out there will come when it hears it. Be ready.

nodes.speaker: mf_corwin
nodes.text: On the mounds, north of the Mere, and on the Mere's own shore. Follow the smell. You won't need to follow it far.

nodes.speaker: mf_corwin
nodes.text: The broken arch at the heart of the barrows. Ring it three times. The sexton used to ring it for every burial. He's still out there, I think. Still doing his rounds. When you ring it, he'll come.

nodes.speaker: mf_corwin
nodes.text: *He listens with his eyes shut. The fen is very quiet.* ...Aye. I can hear it. Nothing walking. *He opens a battered chest and takes out a pair of river-blue greaves.* Carried these out of Skyreach and never had the heart to wear them. They'd rather walk than sit in a box. Take what you need.

nodes.speaker: mf_corwin
nodes.text: One more thing. When the Bellringer went down, he said something. Not to me — to the bell. 'The Heart is hungry.' *He stares into the fire.* I've heard that before. On the mountain. I don't like hearing it twice.

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *On the middle of the boardwalk sits a small, round, pale spirit with its feet in the water. It is wearing — unmistakably — a pair of tiny spectacles. It looks up at you over them.*

nodes.speaker: mf_granny_sen
nodes.text: Don't stare, dearie, it's rude. I'm a lantern that didn't go out. It happens, now and then, when a song isn't finished. You've got wet feet and a good face. That'll do. Sit, if you like. The water's cold, but it's honest.

nodes.speaker: mf_granny_sen
nodes.text: *Granny Sen swings her feet in the water.* Well? Ask, then. I've had a year of nobody to talk to but frogs, and frogs only ever want to talk about flies.

choices.text: Nanami blames herself for the lanterns.

nodes.speaker: mf_granny_sen
nodes.text: Sen. Granny Sen, to the whole fen, whether they were mine or not. Tide-singer of Lowlantern for sixty years. I sang every lantern on this Mere out to the deep marsh, and I never lost one. Not one. *She sniffs.* Until mine.

nodes.speaker: mf_granny_sen
nodes.text: Because my granddaughter — not by blood, by singing, which is better — never finished my song. She got to the last verse and she couldn't. Loved me too much to let go. So here I sit, half-sent. *She lowers her voice.* Don't tell her. She'd only cry, and the fen's wet enough.

nodes.speaker: mf_granny_sen
nodes.text: Course she does. She's a good girl, so she thinks everything's her fault, including the weather. *The spectacles flash.* It's not her song that drowned my light, dearie. It was a hook. I felt it tug, right as she faltered. Find who tied it.

nodes.speaker: mf_granny_sen
nodes.text: Cords. Knotted round the old lantern-stones, down in the mud. Coven work — I'd know Mother Mire's daughters' knots anywhere; I've been untying them for sixty years. Something below the fen wants the lights. The coven sends them down. That's all I know, and more than I'd like.

nodes.speaker: mf_granny_sen
nodes.text: *Granny Sen is standing on the very end of the planks, looking out over the water.* I felt the hooks go. All of them, one after another, like knots coming out of a shawl. *She turns.* So. There's a song I never got to the end of. Somebody had better finish it, before I get used to being a ghost.

choices.text: Nanami. It's time. Sing her the last verse.
I'll sing it. Teach me the words.

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *Nanami walks out past you onto the water — not the boardwalk, the water — and stops in front of the little spirit. Neither of them says anything for a while.* 'Hello, Granny.' 'Hello, little light. You're late.' *Nanami laughs, and it turns into a sob, and the sob turns into the last verse.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *Granny Sen teaches you the last verse. It is short and old and the tune goes somewhere you don't expect. You sing it badly. She laughs so hard her spectacles fall off — and then, as you reach the end, she isn't laughing. She is listening.* 'It never was about the voice, dearie. Only the finishing.'

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *You kneel on the wet planks and say the oldest prayer you know: the one for travellers. Granny Sen bows her head beside you. When you look up, the water around her is full of light, as if every star had come down to walk her home.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *You put your hand in the Mere and ask it, politely, to carry one more light. The water thinks about it — then the whole Mere turns, slow and gentle, like a sleeper rolling over, and the tide comes in under Granny Sen's feet.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *The little spirit rises off the planks, pale and then golden, and drifts out over the Mere. As she passes, the old lantern-stones in the water light one by one — every dark lantern on the Mere, then the floating lights the village never stopped sending, rising up out of the black water all at once.*

nodes.speaker: mf_granny_sen
nodes.text: *Her voice comes from very far off, and very close.* Mind me now. The lights that already went down are still down there, in the deep under the moon-gate — in the Hollow Heart. Mother Mire tends it, and it is hungry. Don't you go after it alone. Take every friend you've got. Then take a few more.

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *The golden light reaches the far side of the Mere, and goes on, out over the reeds, toward the deep marsh where the lost lights gather. Somewhere behind you, in Lowlantern, someone starts to cheer.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *A very old mireling sits on a log in the reeds with a great conch pressed to the side of its head. Its pearl-topped staff leans beside it. It holds up one webbed finger.* Shh. Bloop is listening.

nodes.speaker: mf_oracle_bloop
nodes.text: ...The fen says you are wet, confused, and carrying too many pockets. *It lowers the conch.* The fen is usually right. Bloop is Old Bloop-Who-Listens. Oracle of the Croaking Stones. Formerly.

nodes.speaker: mf_oracle_bloop
nodes.text: *Bloop's golden eyes blink, one, then the other.* Ask. Bloop listens to everything. Even dry-foots.

choices.text: Why do you live out here alone?
What do the coven totems do?
The four totems are broken. They're silent.
The Tidewitch is gone. Here is her pearl.
The Tidewitch is gone. The pearl went down with the water.
(Hold the conch to your ear and listen with Bloop.)

nodes.speaker: mf_oracle_bloop
nodes.text: Bloop said the coven's totems were bad. Bloop said: the totems whisper 'bring us the lights', and lights are not food, lights are people's grandmothers. Gubbagulp said Bloop was bad for saying it. So now Bloop lives with the log. *It pats the log.* The log is a very good listener.

nodes.speaker: mf_oracle_bloop
nodes.text: They whisper. Day and night. 'Bring us the lights, little frogs. Feed the Deep Mother, and the crocolisks will leave your tadpoles alone.' So the young ones steal lantern-glass and cut lantern-lines and feel very brave. *The pearl dims.* Break the totems, dry-foot. Four of them. Then the tribe can hear Bloop again.

nodes.speaker: mf_oracle_bloop
nodes.text: One watches the road into the Croaking Stones, where Gubbagulp sits. One by the Croaker Pool, west. One at the reeds, north of the scouts' camp. One on the old road to the moon-gate. They have skulls with green eyes. You will know them. They will know you.

nodes.speaker: mf_oracle_bloop
nodes.text: Croaking Stones. Croaker Pool. The reeds past the scouts. The gate road. Skulls, antlers, green eyes. *It shudders.* Very rude totems.

nodes.speaker: mf_oracle_bloop
nodes.text: *Bloop presses the conch to its ear for a long time. Then its throat-sac puffs out, enormously, and it lets out one long, happy croak.* Quiet. The fen is quiet. Bloop can hear things again. Bloop can hear... *the eyes go very wide* ...the undertow.

nodes.speaker: mf_oracle_bloop
nodes.text: Under the stone lady — the sunken statue, with her hand in the air — water goes down. Not into the mud. Down stairs. There is an old temple under the fen, and the lights the coven drowns are going down it, down, down, to something that beats. Bloop can hear it beating.

choices.text: A stair under the statue. I'll find it.

nodes.speaker: mf_oracle_bloop
nodes.text: Be careful, dry-foot. Things live in the old temple that were people once, and one that never was. Bloop does not like her song.

nodes.speaker: mf_oracle_bloop
nodes.text: Down. Under the stone lady, into the old temple, to a black well where the water drains away. A witch lives there. Mother Mire's sister, from the sea-road. She drinks the drowned lights and hums, and the undertow carries what's left to the Hollow Heart. *The pearl flickers.* Stop her, and the undertow stops.

choices.text: I'll go down and stop her.

nodes.speaker: mf_oracle_bloop
nodes.text: Bring Bloop her pearl, after. Bloop wants to listen to it. Bloop wants to know what a hundred years of stolen light sounds like. *A pause.* And then Bloop wants to give it back.

nodes.speaker: mf_oracle_bloop
nodes.text: *Bloop holds the pearl to its conch and listens. Very slowly, its eyes fill up.* Lanterns. Hundreds. Singing. *It sets the pearl in the water, and lets go. The pearl sinks, glowing — and then, far out on the fen, a hundred small lights come up out of the reeds and drift away toward the deep marsh.* Thank you, friend.

nodes.speaker: mf_oracle_bloop
nodes.text: *Bloop listens to the conch for a long while.* No more undertow. The water is only water again. *It nods, slowly.* That is enough. That is more than enough.

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *You hold the conch to your ear. The sea, as you'd expect — and then, under it, something else: water running down stone steps, a long way off, under the place where the sunken statue raises her hand.* Bloop nods slowly. 'You hear it too. A stair. Under the stone lady.'

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *You hold the conch to your ear. The sea. Definitely the sea. Possibly also your own pulse.* Bloop watches you with great patience. 'Bloop has been listening for sixty years. Bloop is still learning.'

nodes.speaker: mf_reedcutter_ansel
nodes.text: *A lanky man with a sickle and an armful of reeds nods to you.* Reeds for thatch, reeds for baskets, reeds for the lanterns' wicks. Reeds for everything, except boats. Learned that one the hard way.

choices.text: What's the fen like, past the village?
Seen anything strange out in the reeds?

nodes.speaker: mf_reedcutter_ansel
nodes.text: Road runs west to the Mere, then on over the Heron Bridge into mireling country. Don't leave the road at night. Don't leave the road in the day, either, if you can help it. And if a pretty little light asks you to follow it into the water — it's lying.

nodes.speaker: mf_reedcutter_ansel
nodes.text: *You point out a line of cut reed-stems, too neat for crocolisk teeth.* ...Aye. Somebody's been cutting their own paths through my reed-beds, toward the old statue up north. Small feet. Hat-shaped shadows. I don't go up there any more.

nodes.speaker: mf_reedcutter_ansel
nodes.text: Strange? It's a fen. Everything's strange. That heron's been looking at me funny all week.

nodes.speaker: mf_netmender_orla
nodes.text: *A woman with a mouthful of twine and a lap full of net glares past you, toward Bo's pond.* Over, under, knot. Over, under, knot. Bo, if that crocolisk eats one more of these, I am mending YOU.

choices.text: How long has Bo been losing nets?
Is it true about the lanterns sinking?

nodes.speaker: mf_netmender_orla
nodes.text: Since the spring. Old Gnasher took a liking to them. I think he likes the floats. They're very pretty floats. I painted them.

nodes.speaker: mf_netmender_orla
nodes.text: *She stops mending.* Every one. My dad's went down in the autumn, right in front of me, before the song was halfway. Nanami cried harder than I did. *She goes back to the net, a bit too fast.* Over, under, knot.

nodes.speaker: mf_plip
nodes.text: *A small, extremely confident mireling stands on an upturned crate, beside a tray of shells, pearls and smoked eels.* Plip sells! Plip buys! Plip is Gubbagulp's nephew, so Plip has the best prices. Plip decided this.

nodes.speaker: mf_plip
nodes.text: Very dry. Very tall houses. Everybody waves. *Plip waves back at someone across the pool, enormously.* Lily the small dry-foot says Plip can come to lantern-night. Plip is going to bring an eel.

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text:
*The notice board is a slab of driftwood nailed to two posts. Notes are pinned to it with fish-hooks.*
LOST: one frog. Very handsome. Answers to 'Your Grace'. — Lily.
WANTED: crocolisk tail, fen truffles. Good chowder paid. — H. Brine.
NO LANTERN-NIGHT THIS MONTH EITHER. — the Reeve.
And, in the corner, in very small letters: I am sorry. — N.

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *'I am sorry. — N.' The paper is soft from being handled. Someone has pinned a pressed water-lily beside it, and someone else has written underneath, in a sharp old hand that looks freshly inked though nobody could have: 'Hush, child. Not your fault.'*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *The Low Bell hangs in the broken arch: green bronze, cracked at the lip, with a rope of rotten reed. Names are scratched all round its waist — hundreds of them, in a hundred different hands.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *Fishers, reedcutters, a lamplighter, a 'Tam, aged 6, who could whistle', a 'Sen's Hal, who loved her'. The newest names are not scratched, only written in charcoal, and the rain is taking them.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *The sextons of the Low Bell rang it at every burial on the mounds, so the dead would know where home was if they ever got lost. Three strokes to call them, one to send them back to sleep. Nobody has rung the fourth stroke in years.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *It is a bell. It is old. It is, you are fairly confident, for ringing.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *BONG. The sound goes out across the fen and doesn't come back. BONG. Every frog stops. BONG. Out on the mounds, the mud begins to move — and from the arch's shadow a tall, stooped shape in a sexton's rags steps out, with a bell-rope still round its wrist.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *A great stone face, serene and moss-bearded, sinking into the mire up to its chin. One stone hand is still raised clear of the water, holding a lantern that hasn't been lit in a hundred years.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *The moss under the raised hand is wrong — too smooth, laid like a carpet. You pull it back. Underneath, cut into the stone of the mire itself, a stair goes down, slick and green, into the dark. Somewhere far below, water is running.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *Moss, mud, a startled newt. If the statue is keeping a secret, she is keeping it well.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *The Lady of the Low Lantern. The fen folk built a temple to her before the water rose — a whole temple, with a choir and a bell and a well that was said to reach the sea. When the fen drowned it, they left her hand above the water so the dead could find their way.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *An old statue of an old somebody. She has a kind face. That's something.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *A fairy ring of fat speckled toadstools. In the middle, a flat stone, still warm from something small sitting on it — and a very small, very wet footprint.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *Tiny wet prints, very evenly spaced, as if made by somebody walking with great dignity. They head south-west, toward the willows of the Sinking Mere.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *The prints are fresh. Their owner stopped here to eat four flies and a beetle, sat in the exact middle of the ring for a while (dukes like to be seen), then set off south-west toward the willow on the Mere's west shore.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *Under the willow's hanging fronds, a ring of crushed clover and a scatter of beetle-wings. Somebody has dined here. Somebody with excellent manners.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *The tiny footprints go on — and then, beside them, much larger, flatter, webbed ones. Mireling prints. They head south-west, toward the camps below the Croaking Stones. There is a smell of woodsmoke and, ominously, onions.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *A mireling stewpot bubbles on a reed fire. Sitting on its rim, quite unbothered, is a handsome green frog with a spot on his head like a crown — and beside him, gazing at him adoringly, a plump golden frog wearing a tiny shell necklace.*

choices.text: (Scoop up His Grace and take him home to Lily.)
(Watch the two frogs for a moment.)

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *A mireling stewpot, bubbling quietly. It smells of onions and, faintly, of victory.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *The golden frog croaks, softly. The Duke croaks back. She hops one hop closer. He does not hop away. It is, in its way, the most romantic thing you have ever seen beside a stewpot.*

choices.text: (Lift them both out of the camp and let them go together, free, by the pool.)

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *The Duke is not in danger. The Duke is in love. The golden frog — the mirelings call her Lady Bubbles — was the one who led him here, and nobody has put anyone in the pot. The mirelings were simply warming their feet.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *Two frogs. On a pot. You are reasonably certain of that much.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *His Grace permits himself to be lifted. As you go, he looks back once, over your thumb, at the golden frog on the rim of the pot. She croaks. He doesn't answer.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *You carry them both to the edge of the Croaker Pool and set them on a lily pad. They sit side by side, very close, and do not look at you at all. That seems right.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *Twenty mirelings go quiet at once. In the ring of croaking stones, on a throne of driftwood, sits the biggest frog-person you have ever seen, wearing a crown of river-pearls and a belt of very old, very gold lantern rings.*

nodes.speaker: mf_gubbagulp
nodes.text: DRY-FOOT! Gubbagulp knows why you come. Lantern-folk send you. They say 'Gubbagulp steal our lines, our glass, our lights!' *He puffs up enormously.* Gubbagulp SAYS: the Coven Mothers tell us lights are FOOD for the Deep Mother. Feed the Deep Mother, and the crocolisks leave our tadpoles alone. Is fair trade!

choices.text: The coven's totems are broken. Bloop was right — they lied to you.
The lights don't feed anyone. They're dragged down to something that will eat your tadpoles too, in the end.
Crocolisks hunt open water. Move your spawning pools in under the willows and they'll never find them.
Leave the lantern-folk alone, or I'll leave you without a throne.
Listen. The water itself is crying. You can hear it as well as I can.
Nanami — you speak frog. Tell him.

nodes.speaker: mf_gubbagulp
nodes.text: *Gubbagulp's throat-sac swells to the size of a pumpkin.* LIES! Dry-foot lies! The Coven Mothers PROMISED. *Every spear in the ring comes up.* One more word, and Gubbagulp sits on you.

choices.text: The coven's totems are broken. Bloop was right — they lied to you.
Leave the lantern-folk alone, or I'll leave you without a throne.
Nanami — you speak frog. Tell him.

nodes.speaker: mf_gubbagulp
nodes.text: *He goes very still.* ...Broken? The whispering ones? *Around the ring, mirelings look at each other. One of them, very small, says: 'It IS quieter.'* *Gubbagulp sags on his throne.* Bloop said. Bloop said and Gubbagulp sent Bloop to live with a log.

nodes.speaker: mf_gubbagulp
nodes.text: *Gubbagulp opens his mouth to shout, then closes it. Then opens it again.* ...Under the willows. In the shade. *A long, thoughtful croak.* Crocolisks DO hate the willows. They get the fronds up their noses.

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *You crouch and lay your palm on the water. The tribe goes silent, listening — and then they hear it too: the fen, very faintly, weeping for every light that went down.* Gubbagulp takes off his crown.

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *Nanami steps forward and croaks. It is a long, complicated, surprisingly rude croak. Gubbagulp croaks back, outraged. Nanami croaks again, softer. The whole ring falls silent. Gubbagulp's eyes are very wet.*

nodes.speaker: mf_gubbagulp
nodes.text: *Gubbagulp climbs down off his throne.* The Coven Mothers lied to the tribe. The lights were people's grandmothers. *He pulls the biggest pearl off his crown and holds it out.* Give this to the lantern-folk Reeve. Tell her: no more lines cut. No more glass taken. Gubbagulp is... *he struggles with the word* ...sorry.

nodes.speaker: mf_gubbagulp
nodes.text: And tell her Gubbagulp's nephew Plip wants to sell eels at the lantern-night. Plip is VERY good at eels. *The ring croaks in agreement, deafeningly.*

nodes.speaker: mf_gubbagulp
nodes.text: *Gubbagulp looks at you. Looks at your weapon. Looks at his own very small spear.* ...Gubbagulp thinks the lantern-folk can keep their lines. *He tugs a pearl off his crown and tosses it at your feet, sulkily.* For the Reeve. Go away now.

nodes.speaker: mf_gubbagulp
nodes.text: GUBBAGULP SPEAKS! *He leaps off the throne.* Gubbagulp also HITS!

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *Green fire in a ring of totems, and a cauldron-lantern swinging from a crooked staff. Coven hags in reed cloaks stand round it, humming. In the middle, stirring, is a very old woman with a very long nose and a frog asleep on her hat-brim. She looks up and beams.*

nodes.speaker: mf_auntie_gall
nodes.text: Ah! The lantern-folk's little helpers. Come in, come in, dearies, out of the damp. Auntie's put the kettle on. *She taps the cauldron. It smells of bog-myrtle and old pennies.* You've been cutting my cords. Naughty.

choices.text: Why drown the lanterns? They're people's dead.
Who are you sending the lights to?

nodes.speaker: mf_auntie_gall
nodes.text: *She laughs, warmly, as if you'd said something sweet.* Dead don't need lights, dearie. Dead need nothing at all — that's rather the point of them. But something down below needs them very much, and Mother does love to feed things.

nodes.speaker: mf_auntie_gall
nodes.text: Down through the gate, under the fen, there's a heart that beats where no heart should. Mother tends it. Mother loves it. Every little light we send down makes it beat a bit stronger, and one day it'll beat so strong the whole fen will hear it. Won't that be nice?

choices.text: Not if I can help it.

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *She is not lying, and she is not mad. She is perfectly cheerful, the way a cat is cheerful about a bird. And behind the cheer, under it, you catch something else: she is afraid of whoever she calls Mother.*

nodes.speaker: mf_auntie_gall
nodes.text: *She sighs and sets down her spoon.* Always the same with the helpful ones. Very well. Sit DOWN, dearies. *The cauldron-lantern flares green.* Auntie insists.

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *A stone sending-lantern stands sunk to its shoulders in the black water beside the boardwalk. Its fire-box is full of weed. Something pale is wound round its foot, just below the surface.*

choices.text: (Cut the cord loose and take it.)
(Cut the cord loose and take it.)
(Feel along the lantern's foot under the water.)

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *Under the water your fingers find rope — reed-rope, wet and knotted, wound tight round the lantern's foot and tied off to a river stone. Little frog-bone charms are threaded on it. When you tug, the whole Mere seems to tug back.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *Cold water, soft mud, and something slimy that is probably a weed. Probably.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *You saw through the knotted reed-rope. It comes away with a little shudder, like a held breath let go, and the dark lantern seems to stand a fraction straighter. Frog-bone charms click on the cord in your hand.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *An old lantern-stone, leaning a little, as if something has been pulling at it from below. Its paper window is long gone. Lilies have grown right up to it and then, oddly, stopped.*

choices.text: (Cut the cord loose and take it.)
(Cut the cord loose and take it.)
(Feel along the lantern's foot under the water.)

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *Under the water your fingers find rope — reed-rope, wet and knotted, wound tight round the lantern's foot and tied off to a river stone. Little frog-bone charms are threaded on it. When you tug, the whole Mere seems to tug back.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *Cold water, soft mud, and something slimy that is probably a weed. Probably.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *You saw through the knotted reed-rope. It comes away with a little shudder, like a held breath let go, and the dark lantern seems to stand a fraction straighter. Frog-bone charms click on the cord in your hand.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *A drowned lantern at the end of the cross-walk. Someone has tied a faded ribbon to its roof. Below the water, a skein of something knotted is wrapped round its foot, hung with tiny charms that tick against the stone.*

choices.text: (Cut the cord loose and take it.)
(Cut the cord loose and take it.)
(Feel along the lantern's foot under the water.)

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *Under the water your fingers find rope — reed-rope, wet and knotted, wound tight round the lantern's foot and tied off to a river stone. Little frog-bone charms are threaded on it. When you tug, the whole Mere seems to tug back.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *Cold water, soft mud, and something slimy that is probably a weed. Probably.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *You saw through the knotted reed-rope. It comes away with a little shudder, like a held breath let go, and the dark lantern seems to stand a fraction straighter. Frog-bone charms click on the cord in your hand.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *A coven totem: a driftwood post under an antlered skull, green fire burning in the eye-holes. Up close you can hear it — a whisper, wet and patient: bring us the lights, little ones, bring us the lights.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *You heave at it. The totem groans and leans and does not come down, and the whisper laughs at you. Try again — or try something cleverer.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *The charms are knotted in a pattern that keeps changing as you look at it. Your fingers slip. The green eyes flare.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *You put your shoulder to the post and heave. The skull comes off with a crack like a frozen pond, and the green fire goes out with a hiss.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *One by one you unpick the frog-bone charms. The whisper gets thinner and thinner, and with the last knot it simply stops, mid-word.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *You lay a hand on the post. Something old and patient pushes back — and then gives, all at once, the green fire guttering out like a candle in the rain.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: The totem that watches the road into the Croaking Stones. Silent now.

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: The totem that watches the road into the Croaking Stones. Silent now.

nodes.text: The totem that watches the road into the Croaking Stones. Silent now.

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: The totem by the Croaker Pool, hung with tiny frog-bone charms. Silent now.

nodes.speaker: narrator

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *A coven totem: a driftwood post under an antlered skull, green fire burning in the eye-holes. Up close you can hear it — a whisper, wet and patient: bring us the lights, little ones, bring us the lights.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *You heave at it. The totem groans and leans and does not come down, and the whisper laughs at you. Try again — or try something cleverer.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *The charms are knotted in a pattern that keeps changing as you look at it. Your fingers slip. The green eyes flare.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *You put your shoulder to the post and heave. The skull comes off with a crack like a frozen pond, and the green fire goes out with a hiss.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *One by one you unpick the frog-bone charms. The whisper gets thinner and thinner, and with the last knot it simply stops, mid-word.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *You lay a hand on the post. Something old and patient pushes back — and then gives, all at once, the green fire guttering out like a candle in the rain.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: The totem on the gate road. The reeds lean away from it. Silent now.

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *A crooked lamp-post by the turning to the Shallows, its hook empty and its old jar smashed. Somebody has scratched a little frog-bone sign into the wood.*

choices.text: (Hang one of Obi's lamps on the hook.)

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *The lamp settles on the hook with a click. For a moment nothing — then the wisp-glow wakes in the wick, and a small green light comes up over the road, steady as a heartbeat.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *A giant toadstool taller than a cottage. Its gills glow faintly. Around its foot the soil is dark and soft, and smells of rain on a cellar door.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
nodes.text: *Under the roots, nestled like an egg: a knobbly blue truffle. It smells exactly the way Hettie said it would.*
